title: Intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding
keyIdea: Three kinds of force act between molecules. London (induced dipole) forces act between all molecules and get stronger with more electrons and more surface contact. Permanent dipole–dipole forces add to them when the molecule is polar overall. Hydrogen bonds form only when H is bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. Boiling a simple molecular substance overcomes these forces, not the covalent bonds, so stronger forces mean a higher boiling point.

kid: Molecules pull on each other. These pulls are called intermolecular forces. They are much weaker than the covalent bonds inside a molecule. When a liquid boils, the molecules move apart, but each molecule stays whole.

London forces act between all molecules. Electrons are always moving, so for a moment one side of a molecule has more of them. That makes a small dipole, and it pulls on the next molecule. More electrons mean bigger dipoles. So octane, C₈H₁₈, boils at 126 °C, but methane, CH₄, boils at −162 °C.

Some molecules have a dipole all the time. In HCl, the Cl pulls the shared electrons, so Cl is δ− and H is δ+. The δ+ end of one molecule pulls the δ− end of the next. This is a permanent dipole–dipole force. CO₂ has polar bonds too, but it is straight, so the two dipoles cancel.

The strongest of the three is the hydrogen bond. You need H bonded to N, O or F. That H is very δ+, and it is pulled to a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. This is why water boils at 100 °C, while H₂S boils at −60 °C. It is also why ethanol mixes with water but hexane does not.
adult: This is A-level Chemistry, bonding (for example AQA 3.1.3.7 and OCR A 2.2.2). Students must describe three forces: London (induced dipole) forces, permanent dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. They use them to explain boiling points and how well things mix. They must also draw a hydrogen bond with the partial charges, the lone pair and a straight line.

Key terms: electronegativity, bond polarity, polar molecule, partial charge (δ+ and δ−), induced dipole, permanent dipole, lone pair, hydrogen bond and anomalous. A molecule with polar bonds is only polar if its shape does not cancel them. So CO₂ and CCl₄ are non-polar. London forces grow with the number of electrons and with how much the molecules touch. That is why a straight chain boils higher than a branched one of the same formula.

Common mistakes: saying covalent bonds break when a liquid boils. Thinking London forces act only in non-polar molecules. Giving HCl hydrogen bonds because it has H and a strong pull on electrons. Giving CH₃OCH₃ hydrogen bonds because it has an O. Drawing the bond to an H, or inside one molecule. Be careful with the word strongest: in HCl the London forces are larger than the dipole forces.

In the lab, students tick the forces for five substances, grow and then branch an alkane, and draw two hydrogen bonds. They tap the three odd hydrides on a boiling point plot and compare pairs with almost the same Mr.

familyTip: Put a drop of water and a drop of rubbing alcohol or hand gel on a plate. Which spreads and dries first? Talk about which molecules hold on to each other more strongly, and why water has a high boiling point for such a small molecule.

visual.caption: Can these molecules hydrogen bond to each other? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tick the forces for five substances, grow and branch an alkane, draw hydrogen bonds, find anomalous hydrides and compare similar Mr.

practice.prompt: Which forces act between HCl molecules?
choices: London forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces
practice.hint: London forces act between all molecules. Is H bonded to N, O or F?
practice.explain: HCl is polar, so dipole–dipole forces act, and London forces act between all molecules. H is bonded to Cl, not N, O or F, so there are no hydrogen bonds.

practice.prompt: An alkane has {n} carbon atoms, so its formula is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. How many electrons does one molecule have? (C has 6, H has 1.)
practice.hint: Count 6 for each C and 1 for each of the 2n + 2 H atoms.
practice.explain: 6 × {n} + (2 × {n} + 2) = {=8*n+2} electrons. More electrons mean stronger London forces and a higher boiling point.

practice.prompt: Ethanol (Mr 46) boils at 78 °C, but propane (Mr 44) boils at −42 °C. Why?
choices: Ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds; propane has only London forces
practice.hint: The Mr values are close. What does ethanol have that propane does not?
practice.explain: With similar Mr the London forces are similar. Ethanol's O–H group lets hydrogen bonds form, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

practice.prompt: The group 16 trend would put the boiling point of water at about −{t} °C. Water really boils at 100 °C. How many degrees higher is that?
practice.hint: From −{t} °C up to 0 °C, then from 0 °C up to 100 °C.
practice.explain: {t} + 100 = {=100+t} degrees higher. This big jump is caused by hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

pool.prompt: CO₂ has two polar C=O bonds. Which forces act between CO₂ molecules?
pool.hint: CO₂ is linear. What happens to the two bond dipoles?
pool.explain: The two dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so CO₂ is non-polar and only London forces act.

pool.prompt: Which substance has hydrogen bonds between its molecules?
pool.hint: Look for H bonded directly to N, O or F.
pool.explain: NH₃ has H on N and a lone pair on N. In CH₃OCH₃ every H is on C, and in HCl the H is on Cl.

pool.prompt: Pentane boils at 36 °C and 2,2-dimethylpropane at 9.5 °C. Both are C₅H₁₂. Why the difference?
choices: The straight chain has more surface contact, so stronger London forces
pool.hint: Same formula, same number of electrons. What is different about the shape?
pool.explain: The ball-shaped isomer touches its neighbours less, so its London forces are weaker and it boils lower.

pool.prompt: A molecule X₂ is made of two atoms with {z} electrons each. How many electrons does one X₂ molecule have?
pool.hint: There are two atoms in the molecule.
pool.explain: 2 × {z} = {=2*z} electrons. More electrons mean stronger London forces: from F₂ (18 electrons) to I₂ (106), boiling points rise.

pool.prompt: When water boils, what is overcome?
choices: Hydrogen bonds and other forces between molecules
pool.hint: Is steam still made of H₂O molecules?
pool.explain: Steam is still H₂O. Only the forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds stay.

pool.prompt: In a drawing of a hydrogen bond between two water molecules, where should the dotted line go?
choices: From a δ+ H on one molecule to a lone pair on O of another
From H on one molecule to H on another
Between O and H inside one molecule
pool.hint: Which parts carry opposite partial charges, on different molecules?
pool.explain: The δ+ H is attracted to a lone pair on the δ− O of a different molecule, in a nearly straight line O–H···O.

pool.prompt: Why does ethanol mix with water, but hexane does not?
choices: Ethanol can hydrogen bond with water molecules
Hexane is too heavy to mix
pool.hint: What can ethanol's O–H group do with water?
pool.explain: Ethanol's O–H group forms hydrogen bonds with water. Hexane only has London forces, so water molecules stay bonded to each other.

pool.prompt: HF boils at 20 °C and HCl at −85 °C. A sample of HF is at {t} °C. How many degrees must it warm to reach its boiling point?
pool.explain: 20 − {t} = {=20-t} degrees. HF boils much higher than HCl because of hydrogen bonds.
